archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (pass-first)
archetype.definition: A roughly average team whose point differential and efficiency say it should have a couple more wins, carried by Stroud's passing while last year's elite defense has turned boom-or-bust.

report.headline: A .500 team wearing a 2-5 record, undone by close losses and deep balls
report.take:
This is not last year's Texans. The 2025 team went 12-5 on the back of the league's second-best defense by EPA allowed and an offense that ranked 22nd. This year the identity has flipped. C.J. Stroud has started every game behind a line that ranks 6th in pressure rate allowed, and the passing offense is 11th in EPA per play. The defense has slid to 24th, and that slide is the biggest change on the roster.

The record overstates how bad the team is. Houston has been outscored by just 5 points, a margin that implies 4.2 wins rather than two, and its wins over expected rank 31st. It has won only 20% of its one-score games. Every loss except the 6-20 game against Cincinnati was decided by one score. Turnovers do not explain it: the offense has given the ball away only 3 times, and the turnover margin is positive. What has cost them is the margins of close games. They rank 24th in red-zone touchdown rate allowed, 25th in penalties per game, 29th in fourth-down aggressiveness and 20th in special teams EPA. Close games tend to even out over time, but those habits are real and they cost points every week.

The defense is stranger than its rank. It is 7th in success rate allowed and leads the league with 21 sacks, so it wins most snaps. It is also dead last in explosive pass rate allowed and 25th in deep-pass EPA, so the snaps it loses go for big plays. On offense, the run game drags everything down: 3.3 yards per carry (28th) and 2.24 yards before contact. That leaves the offense living on Stroud. The Giants loss shows what happens when he is held down. Houston was a 10-point favorite, threw for only 153 yards, gave up 188 rushing yards and lost in overtime.

From here, a season that looks lost is really a team at about .500 sitting two games under it. The AFC South is weak enough that this still matters, with Jacksonville at 4-2 and Indianapolis level with Houston at 2-5. Better close-game luck should come. Whether it turns into a real climb depends on two things: the safeties getting healthy, and the run game giving Stroud anything at all.

strengths.title: Stroud's clean-pocket passing game
strengths.body: The pass offense ranks 11th in EPA per play because Stroud is rarely under duress. The line is 6th in pressure rate allowed and 5th in QB hit rate allowed. He has also protected the ball, with only three offensive turnovers all season. A line that pass-protects this well while failing as a run-blocking unit makes this a sustainable, if one-dimensional, engine.

strengths.title: League-best sack production
strengths.body: Houston leads the league with 21 sacks and ranks 4th in sack rate. That production comes even though its overall pressure rate is only mid-pack (15th), which means the rushers are finishing the pressures they get. Paired with the 7th-best success rate allowed, this front wins most downs. Finishing rates like this can cool off, but the down-to-down success suggests the front itself is good.

strengths.title: Record trails the point differential
strengths.body: A -5 point differential implies 4.2 wins, and the 20% one-score win rate is the kind of number that usually drifts back toward even. The turnover margin is positive, so this is not a team giving games away with the ball. Expect more of the coin flips to land their way.

concerns.title: Explosive passes, now without both safeties
concerns.body: The defense allows the highest explosive pass rate in the league and ranks 25th in deep-pass EPA. That is why a unit 7th in success rate ranks 24th in EPA. Both starting safeties are listed out: Jalen Pitre at 92% of snaps and Reed Blankenship at 86%. Until they return, the leak in the back end is more likely to widen than close, and this is a real flaw rather than noise.

concerns.title: A run game that can't stand up
concerns.body: The team averages 3.3 yards per carry (28th) with only 2.24 yards before contact and a 26th-ranked run success rate. The cause is mostly the blocking, not game script. David Montgomery is also out, which leaves Woody Marks to carry the load. Without a run threat, a good pass defense can make the offense one-dimensional, as Cincinnati and the Giants did.

concerns.title: Self-inflicted damage in tight games
concerns.body: Houston ranks 25th in penalties per game and 28th in line penalties, with 508 penalty yards in seven games. It is also 24th in red-zone touchdown rate allowed and 29th in fourth-down go rate. The run defense is a further soft spot at 29th in rush EPA allowed. None of this is luck. It is why the close games keep slipping away, and it will keep costing points until it is cleaned up.

trend.note: Three straight close losses opened the year around a 6-20 dud. Then came a blowout of Tennessee and a road win at Jacksonville, both convincing. The overtime home loss to the Giants as a 10-point favorite erased that momentum heading into the bye.

nextGame.headline: Rested Texans visit the winless Chargers and the league's worst offense
nextGame.body:
Houston comes off its bye with two weeks of rest to face a 0-6 Chargers team whose offense ranks last in EPA, last in pass EPA and 30th in run EPA. That offense leans on the run more than anyone, ranking last in pass rate over expected, behind a line that is 31st in sack rate allowed and last in QB hits allowed. The trouble is the other side. The Chargers' defense is legitimate: 10th in EPA allowed, 7th against the pass, 6th on third down and 10th in the red zone. It will test a Houston offense that can't run the ball. No line has been posted.

Availability is the swing. Both Houston starting safeties, Pitre and Blankenship, are listed out with return estimates of game day, so their status is genuinely uncertain. Montgomery is out, and Jaylin Noel was seen in a walking boot. For the Chargers, Derwin James, Joe Alt, Tre' Harris and Ladd McConkey all carry questionable tags. McConkey has been practicing in a no-contact jersey after a concussion.

waysToWin.title: Pass rush feasts on a leaky line
waysToWin.body: Houston's league-leading sack total meets a Chargers line that ranks 31st in sack rate and last in QB hits allowed. If the front forces passing downs, drive-killing sacks should come in bunches against an offense that already can't throw efficiently. This is the clearest edge on the field.

waysToWin.title: Spread it past the WR1
waysToWin.body: The Chargers have held opposing WR1s well under their averages, ranking 4th by that measure. Their WR2s, however, have scored well over, ranking 31st. Houston's targets are already spread among Schultz, Hutchinson, Collins and others, so Stroud can work away from the strength of the coverage. Early-season positional numbers are thin, but this matchup fits how Houston already distributes the ball.

waysToWin.title: Win the turnover margin
waysToWin.body: The Chargers sit 30th in turnover differential, while Houston's offense has turned it over only three times all season. A clean game from Stroud plus one or two takeaways can supply the short fields that this tough Chargers defense otherwise won't allow.

waysToLose.title: Chargers grind it on the ground
waysToLose.body: The Chargers run more than anyone, and Houston's run defense ranks 29th in rush EPA allowed. The Giants just ran for 188 yards on it. If the Chargers stay ahead of the chains on the ground, they keep Houston's pass rush out of the game and shorten it into the kind of one-score finish Houston keeps losing.

waysToLose.title: Stalled offense against a good pass defense
waysToLose.body: The Chargers are 7th in pass EPA allowed and 6th on third down. Houston's 28th-ranked yards per carry gives Stroud no help, and Montgomery is out. Cincinnati and the Giants both shut this offense down by taking away the pass. A repeat turns the game into a low-scoring slog against a team with nothing to lose.

waysToLose.title: One deep ball with backup safeties
waysToLose.body: A bad Chargers passing game can still produce a single explosive play, and Houston allows them at the league's worst rate. If both starting safeties sit, one coverage bust could decide a tight game. Add the penalties and red-zone defense that have already cost close games.

nextGame.watch: How the Chargers fare on early-down runs. If Houston's front stops them and forces passing downs, the league's top pass rush gets to face one of the league's worst pass-protecting lines.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying team is about .500, and the close-game record should improve. A 20% one-score win rate and wins over expected near the bottom of the league rarely hold. The schedule offers chances. Indianapolis and Tennessee at home are divisional games against bottom-tier offenses. Trips to Washington and Philadelphia face struggling teams. The road games at Cleveland and Pittsburgh, against top-seven defenses, are where this run-starved offense is most likely to bog down.

What should hold up is Stroud's efficient, low-turnover passing behind good protection, along with a pass rush that wins downs. What may fade is the sack pace, which is outrunning a mid-pack pressure rate. The real threats to a climb are the explosive-pass leak, worse without the safeties, and penalty and red-zone habits that aren't luck. Expect wins to come in bunches against the soft part of the schedule, leaving Houston on the edge of the AFC South race rather than out of it.
swingFactors: Return of safeties Pitre and Blankenship
Any functional run game without Montgomery
Close-game execution: penalties and red-zone defense

confidence.note: Seven games of close-game noise, with two starting safeties out.
